Elite Colleges Can Give You an Investing Lesson
 
Plus, bonds got their mojo back
 

Thursday was stressful for people who checked their portfolios—especially if they owned hard-hit Meta or data-center stocks. But it was reassuringly normal in another way: The Treasury market acted like it used to, providing an offset. They had their best day in more than a year with the 10-year note’s yield falling sharply to well below 5%. Stock futures are mixed ahead of the open and oil is higher again on Middle East security jitters.

 

​📈 Follow our live markets data and coverage.

10/23/2026, 6:38:46 AM ET
 
 
 

It’s vanity

 

You don’t have to be a rocket scientist to make average investing returns. Sometimes it helps not being one.

 

The Massachusetts Institute of Technology says that its massive endowment, managed by executives who earn more than the university’s president, earned 10.3% during its fiscal year ended in June. That’s less than half of what an S&P 500 index fund earned.

 

MIT’s results are more surprising during a tech boom that it might seem uniquely equipped to harness. Harvard and Stanford’s endowments, which held big stakes in SpaceX acquired before its IPO, jumped 27.1% and 31.7%, respectively. The University of North Carolina, which had more than a tenth of its endowment in that stock, did even better.

 

As uplifting as one-year moonshots are, big college endowments offer tuition-free lessons these days about how not to invest. Special access to mostly so-so but costly private equity, hedge and venture-capital funds has seen their returns lag what mom and pop investors could have made over the past decade. Meanwhile, infrequent fund value updates give endowments a false appearance of stability. Only 14% of Harvard’s is directly in publicly traded stocks and just 3% in bonds.

 

Once upon a time, the “Yale Model,” pioneered by that university’s chief investment officer David Swensen, got great results this way. He could take a very long view, and illiquid investments were cheaper back then.

 

Now, though, those funds are seeking money from a new audience—you. Lobbyists are pushing to allow alternative investments into 401(k) plans and already offer them outside retirement accounts. Broker Robinhood earlier this year listed its first “Venture Fund,” which holds stakes in unlisted companies such as OpenAI, Oura and in now-public SpaceX.

 

“Opening up private markets will resolve one of the greatest longstanding inequities in capital markets today,” said Robinhood CEO Vlad Tenev.

 

That fund sports a 3.1% expense ratio, 100 times the cost of an S&P 500 index fund.

 

An annual report of university business administrators from 2025 points out an interesting divide between the haves and have-nots of higher education. Institutions with assets of less than $50 million allocated 13% of their portfolios to “alternatives.” At the other end of the spectrum, those with more than $5 billion in assets allocated 63%.

 

Why? Partly it’s vanity, according to investing veteran Richard Ennis. Harvard University gets better access than Harding University. Surely their money should be managed by the best and brightest.

 

But the only sure thing is expenses. Ennis writes that endowment managers “mostly operate as if nothing has changed” since Swensen’s heyday. Allocating 60% to alternatives costs them about 3% annually, or about what Robinhood charges, according to his math.

 

Even those of us who couldn’t get into MIT can spot the problem.

Telecoms majors slid premarket at the prospect of increased competition, with AT&T and Verizon both falling by more than 3%.

 

↘️Kering: The Paris-listed stock tumbled after the Gucci owner recorded a fall in revenue amid waning demand for luxury goods.

 

↘️ Volvo Car: Shares in the Swedish automaker plunged after it said it would cut around 6% of its workforce in a bid to to make savings totaling $500 million.

 

↘️Moderna: Shares fell premarket, on course to extend yesterday’s plunge sparked by the appearance on social media of closely guarded details relating to a cancer-vaccine study.
